title: After the Exchange Study Abroad at Lund University
paragraphs: From March to April I studied at Lund University in Sweden and was allowed to do clinical clerkships at local hospitals. It was my first time living abroad, but I learned a great deal, and it was a wonderful opportunity to have experiences I had never had. Here I report on my two months of study abroad experience.

Lund University is a comprehensive university headquartered in the town of Lund in southern Sweden, founded in 1666 and with a history of over 300 years. Its affiliated hospital, Skåne University Hospital, has facilities in Lund and also in the neighboring city of Malmö, and I did my clerkships at the hospital in Malmö throughout the two months.

For the first four weeks I rotated through infectious diseases. In Sweden, because of the history of major infectious disease epidemics in the early twentieth century, infectious diseases is established as a specialty. However, most infectious diseases are treated in internal medicine, and the infectious diseases department where I did my clerkship handled complex cases with comorbidities and care for specific diseases such as tuberculosis. For the clerkship, I was attached to one resident per week, joined the review meeting from 8 a.m., and then accompanied the resident on rounds. Each doctor was in charge of about six to seven patients, and it was impressive that they did rounds carefully, spending more than ten minutes on each patient. The review meetings and rounds were in Swedish, so I could not understand what was being said on the spot, but when writing charts and at other times the doctor explained to me in English, and I could understand the patients' diseases and treatment plans. Also, once a week the supervising teacher set up a one-on-one teaching session, and I was able to acquire basic knowledge about infectious diseases. At that time, I could also discuss, if only briefly, differences in the frequency of infectious diseases between Japan and Sweden and the resulting differences in prevention and treatment, which was a meaningful time. In addition, I was allowed to observe outpatient clinics. In the outpatient clinic they did post-discharge follow-up for tuberculosis, treatment of viral hepatitis and so on, and I was also allowed to actually perform elastography to assess liver fibrosis on patients.

Next, I did four more weeks in the vascular unit. The vascular unit is a department made up of vascular surgeons, several physicians and radiologists, and in the clerkship I observed surgeries and endovascular treatment by the vascular surgeons. Endovascular treatment in particular is said to have one of the highest volumes in Europe, and I could observe various procedures such as endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) for aortic aneurysms and percutaneous angioplasty for peripheral arterial occlusion and stenosis. As for EVAR, in addition to standard EVAR, performed for aortic aneurysms below the renal artery bifurcation, fenestrated endovascular aneurysm repair (FEVAR) was also performed for juxtarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms, where the lesion is located more proximally. In Japan, surgery is often chosen for juxtarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms, so it was a valuable opportunity to observe a treatment I had never seen. I had the impression that FEVAR is technically difficult, but experienced doctors finished the procedure in a short time, and I sensed the skilled technique cultivated through many treatments. As for other procedures and surgeries, the treatment of thoracic outlet syndrome was impressive. In thoracic outlet syndrome a thrombus can form in the subclavian vein, and the treatment consisted of several stages: catheter-directed thrombolysis, evaluation of its effect by angiography, and, a few days later, resection of the first rib together with balloon dilation and stent placement of the subclavian vein. Until I observed the procedure I had no image of it as a disease treated by vascular surgery, and I was surprised that the vascular surgeons also performed not only thrombolysis but also rib removal. But by actually seeing the treatment, I could understand that each stage is related and that it is important for the vascular surgeon to treat the whole course consistently.

In this study abroad, I was able not only to learn about medical practice in the real clinical setting but also to find differences from Japan in systems. For example, regarding doctors' work patterns, in the department where I did my clerkship there was a system to avoid long working hours, such as separating day shifts and on-call night shifts, and I felt that work-style reform is advanced, just as I had imagined of Sweden before the study abroad. On the other hand, from the patients' standpoint, access to medical care is better in Japan, and I think it is an environment in which tests and treatment can be received easily. It is not a matter of which is better, but I felt that it is important at least to know the systems of other countries and compare them with one's own. Being able to gain such a social perspective, even a little, is also one of the gains of this study abroad.

As a change compared with before the study abroad, I also came to feel the importance of learning proactively. I had an opportunity to do a clerkship with local medical students for about one week in infectious diseases, and I was strongly stimulated to see them actively communicating with the doctors and asking about points they did not understand. Unlike until now, when I studied according to a fixed curriculum, after graduating from medical school I think an attitude of proactively acquiring knowledge and skills will be required. I have tended to be strongly passive in clerkships until now, but I want to remember what I felt on this study abroad and work hard in future clerkships and in initial residency after graduation.

Although this exchange study abroad was a short period of two months, it was truly fulfilling. I express my deep gratitude to everyone at Lund University and Skåne University Hospital, who gave me great support and guidance. I also received warm support and advice from Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and everyone in the International Collaboration Office in preparing for the study abroad, and I am deeply grateful. Many professors gave me guidance in the pre-departure training, and I sincerely thank them. Finally, I thank 吉田さん, who also studied at Lund University, and the other 12 members who studied hard together toward the study abroad. Thank you.
